The field $\phi_t$ evolves with temporal parameter $\rho_T$ and innovation scale $\tau^2$ on fixed geographical graph $W$. $D$ contains neighbour counts and $Q^{-}$ denotes the constrained intrinsic covariance construction. Allocation priors also specify temporal dependence; the equations show the latent structure, not all hyperpriors.

Both smooth variation and localised intercept patterns can evolve over time.

**Limitations:** Group assignments need not form contiguous regions. The model does not estimate an unrestricted adjacency graph at each time point; graph optimisation and dynamically sampled edges are separate constructions.

::: callout-warning
## Operational warning: spatio-temporal allocations

`ST.CARlocalised()` uses MCMC; a standard single INLA fit does not integrate its unknown group allocations. Match the intercept, data ordering and fixed-graph requirements in the [CARBayesST manual](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/CARBayesST/CARBayesST.pdf); the [vignette, equation (10)](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/CARBayesST/vignettes/CARBayesST.pdf) specifies the hierarchy.
:::

**Configuration example.** Documentation: [CARBayesST ST.CARlocalised](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/CARBayesST/CARBayesST.pdf) and [hierarchy in the vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/CARBayesST/vignettes/CARBayesST.pdf).

## Bayesian Model Evaluation and Prior Sensitivity

### Pointwise WAIC and Spatial Autocorrelation

Predictive evaluation should match the intended task. Pointwise LOO assesses prediction of a held-out observation when the remaining observations, including its neighbours, are available. This is appropriate for interpolation but can be optimistic for transfer to unobserved neighbourhoods.

#### Recommended Alternative: Spatial Block & Leave-Neighbourhood-Out Cross-Validation

As a general recommendation, consider spatial blocks or leave-neighbourhood-out validation when assessing transfer beyond observed neighbourhoods. For a held-out set $N(i)$, the target is $p(\mathbf y_{N(i)}\mid\mathbf y_{-N(i)})$. Choose blocks to reflect the intended use, and distinguish these scores from pointwise CPO/LOO. Boundary recovery requires separate assessment (Vehtari et al., 2017; Roberts et al., 2017).

For pointwise diagnostics, R-INLA provides `control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE)`. These options do not perform spatial block cross-validation; held-out groups and their scoring target require a separate specification.

**CPO (Conditional Predictive Ordinate)**: The leave-one-out cross-validated predictive density $p(y_i \mid \mathbf{y}_{-i})$, approximated by INLA using the fitted model. Unusually small values indicate poor leave-one-out predictive fit; they do not alone establish high leverage or explain the discrepancy.

**LCPO (Logarithmic CPO)**: Here this label denotes the negative mean log-CPO score:

$$
\text{LCPO} = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log(\text{CPO}_i)
$$

Lower LCPO indicates superior predictive accuracy. This is the negated mean of log-CPO values; do not confuse with LPML ($= \sum \log(\text{CPO}_i)$, where higher is better).

**PIT (Probability Integral Transform)**: A predictive calibration diagnostic. For continuous outcomes, a correctly specified predictive CDF evaluated at the observation is uniformly distributed. Histogram shapes can suggest dispersion problems, but need interpretation with finite-sample variability and dependence in mind.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Technical Note: PIT for Count Outcomes

For discrete outcomes, $F_i(y_i)$ is not continuously uniform. A randomized transform is $U_i=F_i(y_i^-)+V_i[F_i(y_i)-F_i(y_i^-)]$, with $V_i\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$. Check the software's PIT convention and account for dependence among leave-one-out diagnostics before applying uniformity tests (Dunn & Smyth, 1996).
:::

**WAIC / DIC**: Compare models fitted to the same response and evaluation target. Interpret score differences alongside their uncertainty and practical relevance; fixed cutoffs such as $\Delta\mathrm{WAIC}>4$ or $\Delta\mathrm{DIC}>5$ are not universal evidence thresholds. WAIC and LOO also require care over the pointwise likelihood and which latent effects are integrated out (Vehtari, Gelman, & Gabry, 2017).

**Residual Moran's** $I$: Residual spatial autocorrelation can indicate remaining model structure, but a nonsignificant result does not establish independence or adequate fit. Interpret `spdep::moran.test()` in light of the chosen residuals and test assumptions; posterior predictive comparisons of spatial discrepancies provide a complementary check (Gelman et al., 2020).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Operational note: predictive diagnostics

Inspect `result$cpo$failure`; investigate positive flags and extreme log-score contributions using `inla.cpo()` or held-out refits. See the [R-INLA FAQ](https://www.r-inla.org/faq). For spatial groups, consult the [`inla.group.cv()` vignette](https://www.inla.r-inla-download.org/r-inla.org/doc/vignettes/AA-group-cv.html); groupwise predictive ordinates and joint block log scores are different targets.
:::

## Software Implementation and Workflow

R-INLA provides deterministic approximate inference for many latent Gaussian models discussed here, while the worked example and several boundary models use MCMC. Its computational advantage depends on the latent structure, hyperparameter dimension and approximation settings (Rue, Martino, and Chopin, 2009). The `inlabru` package provides higher-level tools for fitting spatial models with INLA.

**When R-INLA applies**: Suitable latent Gaussian specifications include BYM, BYM2, Leroux, proper CAR, SPDE and spline models. Feasibility also depends on implementation and hyperparameter dimension. Post-hoc areal wombling is possible by computing contrasts from joint approximate posterior draws after fitting the field.

Prior predictive checks simulate outcomes from the full prior, with the application's covariates and offsets, to assess plausible counts, risks and spatial contrasts. Posterior predictive checks simulate replicated outcomes from posterior states and compare features such as zeros, tails and spatial differences (Gelman et al., 2020). Neither a universal log-risk range nor a fixed percentage cutoff establishes adequacy.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Operational note: posterior predictive simulation

Fit with `control.compute=list(config=TRUE)` to use `inla.posterior.sample()`. It returns approximate posterior states, not replicated observations; simulate those from the observation likelihood for each draw. See the [posterior-sampling documentation](https://www.r-inla.org/learnmore/docs/reference/posterior.sample.html).
:::

# To End: Methodological Challenges and Advanced Perspectives

## Spatial Confounding and Model Selection

Spatially structured covariates and random effects can compete to explain the same variation, changing coefficient estimates and uncertainty (Hodges & Reich, 2010). Restricted Spatial Regression (RSR) is one proposed response, projecting the random field onto the orthogonal complement of the covariate space (Hughes & Haran, 2013):

$$
\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\mathrm{RSR}}=P_X^\perp\boldsymbol{\phi},
\qquad P_X^\perp=I-X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top,
$$ 

assuming $X$ has full column rank. Be aware, this changes the model; it does not guarantee unbiased coefficients or genuine residual boundaries.

RSR should not be a default correction. Khan and Calder (2022) demonstrate adverse coverage and sign-error behaviour in studied settings, while Donegan (2025) critiques the conceptual framing of spatial confounding. Specify the target association or causal estimand and distinguish boundaries in total risk from boundaries in residual effects before choosing restrictions.

## Prior Sensitivity and Robustness

**Penalised Complexity (PC) priors** express shrinkage towards a stated base model (Simpson et al., 2017):

1.  **Standard deviation**: $P(\sigma>U_\sigma)=\alpha_\sigma$ gives an exponential prior on $\sigma$ with rate $\lambda_\sigma=-\log(\alpha_\sigma)/U_\sigma$, shrinking towards no random effect.
2.  **BYM2 mixing parameter**: $P(\phi<U_\phi)=\alpha_\phi$ calibrates the graph-specific PC prior, with base model $\phi=0$. This is not a generic PC-prior formula for every spatial correlation parameter.

PC priors are an interpretable option, not an automatic guarantee of robustness. Gamma$(0.001,0.001)$ shape–rate priors on precision should not be labelled non-informative: the induced inverse-gamma variance prior has a heavy tail, and posterior sensitivity depends on the likelihood and scale. Document and assess the resulting prior predictions (see Gelman et al., 2020).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Technical note: prior sensitivity

Refit across substantively plausible prior settings and compare effect sizes, uncertainty, predictive behaviour, and boundary decisions. Vary both scale and mixing priors where relevant. Overlapping marginal intervals alone do not establish robustness; report changes in the conclusions of interest (Gelman et al., 2020).
:::

## Computational Complexity and Large Datasets

### Iterative Pseudo-INLA for Adaptive Adjacency Graphs

The algorithm and social-frontier criterion are specified under **Localised Autocorrelation Model** above (Lee and Mitchell, 2013; Dean et al., 2019). Its cost includes repeated conditional fits; the fewer-than-five iterations reported by Dean et al. concern their applications, not a universal convergence rate. Graph-selection uncertainty remains outside the final conditional posterior.

Dong et al. (2020) extend locally adaptive modelling to multilevel logistic data using MCMC with Pólya–Gamma augmentation.

For dense Gaussian-process covariance matrices, direct factorisation typically costs $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$. Sparse GMRF factorisation depends on graph structure, ordering, and fill-in; approximately $\mathcal{O}(N^{3/2})$ is a useful two-dimensional lattice benchmark, not a rate for every graph or complete INLA fit (Rue & Held, 2005; Bakka et al., 2018).

## Synthesis & Comparative Recommendations

**Conceptual comparison**

| Methodology | Domain | Primary Mechanism | Boundary Target |
|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|
| **Curvilinear Wombling** | Continuous surface | Gradients ($\nu>1$); Matérn curvature ($\nu>2$) | Rapid directional change |
| **Global CAR / BYM2** | Areal graph | Posterior contrasts | Risk or residual differences; smoothing can attenuate jumps |
| **Dissimilarity CAR** | Areal graph | Binary covariate thresholding (Lee–Mitchell) | Removed edges |
| **Spatial DP / MARDP** | Areal graph | Shared atoms and posterior equality | Differences between latent effects |
| **Iterative Pseudo-INLA** | Areal graph | Deterministic graph updates and conditional fits | Selected graph breaks |
| **ABI-DAGAR Flow** | Areal graph | Covariate boundary rule and neural posterior approximation | Boundary probabilities under the fitted model |

**Computation and software**

| Methodology | Computational Considerations | Software |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| **Curvilinear Wombling** | Dense GP factorisation typically $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ | nimblewomble |
| **Global CAR / BYM2** | Sparse graph factorisation; structure-dependent cost | R-INLA, Stan |
| **Dissimilarity CAR** | Model- and sampler-dependent | CARBayes |
| **Spatial DP / MARDP** | Specialised MCMC | Authors' implementation |
| **Iterative Pseudo-INLA** | Repeated sparse fits; no general linear-time guarantee | R-INLA with iterative updates |
| **ABI-DAGAR Flow** | Training plus graph-dependent preprocessing and sampling | BayesFlow / authors' implementation |

# Example Bayesian Workflow Plan (Betancourt and Gelman)

The following is an illustrative synthesis informed by Betancourt (2020), Gelman et al. (2020), and McElreath (2020), rather than a workflow reproduced verbatim from a single source.

1.  Generative Architecture of Spatial Latent Gaussian Models (LGMs):

    - Level 1 (Observation Likelihood): Conditional independence given the linear predictor 'η' and likelihood hyperparameters 'θ₁'.
    - Level 2 (Structured Latent Gaussian Field): A Gaussian latent field; a GMRF representation uses a sparse precision matrix 'Q(θ₂)'. Sparsity and geographical adjacency are model-specific, not requirements of every Gaussian process.
    - Level 3 (Hyperparameter Hierarchy): Hyperpriors for variance, correlation and mixing parameters; INLA is most practical when numerical integration remains manageable.

2.  The Ten-Stage Conceptual Workflow:

    - Stage 1 (Formulation): Distinguishing area-level continuous outcomes, bounded proportions, and overdispersed counts.

    - Stage 2 (Penalized Complexity Priors): Eliciting tail probabilities from base models ('σ = 0', 'φ = 0').

    - Stage 3 (Spatial Graph Topology): Graph validation, Queen contiguity matrices, and handling disconnected island enclaves.

    - Stage 4 (Prior Predictive Checks): Domain-bounded generative simulations prior to empirical confrontation.

    - Stage 5 (Deterministic Laplace Inference): Approximating hyperparameter marginals 'p(θ\|y)' and latent conditional posteriors 'p(xᵢ\|θ,y)'.

    - Stage 6 (Spatial Cross-Validation): Evaluating predictive leave-one-out densities (CPO / LCPO) and Leave-Group-Out Cross-Validation (LGOCV) under spatial autocorrelation.

    - Stage 7 (Calibration & Model Criticism): Assessing predictive calibration (with discrete-outcome PIT conventions) and joint posterior predictive replications.

    - Stage 8 (Prior Sensitivity Sweeps): Hyperparameter sweeps across tight, moderate, and loose specifications.

    - Stage 9 (Information Criteria & Parsimony): WAIC and DIC penalization by effective parameter complexity ('p_eff').

    - Stage 10 (Posterior Synthesis & Uncertainty): Report posterior intervals and boundary uncertainty; interpret variance allocation using the actual parameterisation and area-specific variances.

3.  Methodological Caveats in Spatial Latent Modeling:

    - Numerical Approximation Stability: Investigate CPO integration failures and validate problematic values with revised integration or held-out refits.
    - Spatial Graph Scaling ('scale.model = TRUE'): Improve scale comparability across graphs; the mixing prior and node-specific variances can still depend on graph structure.
    - Identifiability & Constraints: Centre intrinsic fields as required; imposing a sum-to-zero constraint on a proper field changes its prior and does not by itself resolve spatial confounding.
    - Spatial Confounding & Variance Allocation: Assess how covariates and spatial random effects compete to explain variation; specify the association or causal estimand before choosing restrictions.
    - Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP): Multi-scale boundary buffering sensitivity.
